recon_agent: papers-recon-C (gap-point hunter: source-uncited mechanisms with paper roots)
scope: Mechanisms whose ALGORITHM has published/spec roots but where the C++/MLIR/Python source does NOT write a citation (or cites only a vendor-doc URL).
Read the implementation under instances/triton/source to confirm algorithm form, then web-verified the literature lineage.
discipline_note: arXiv ids / DOIs web-verified via arxiv.org, ACM DL, OCP, and the MICRO/POPL/SODA program records (title + authors + venue/year matched). Papers whose id/venue is written verbatim in source are marked source-cited. Where NO formal paper exists (e.g. LinearLayout is an internal construction), that is stated honestly as unverified-candidate — no citation is fabricated. 'GAP' in where_used flags mechanisms the source uses but does not cite.

findings.topic: Triton itself: the tile abstraction + tiled-IR compiler (foundational)
findings.mechanism_evidence: The whole book's object. Confirmed the tile-centric language/IR in python/triton/language and lib/Dialect/Triton*. README.md:19 explicitly asks readers to cite the MAPL2019 paper.
findings.source_excerpt: README.md:19  'The foundations of this project are described in the following MAPL2019 publication: Triton: An Intermediate Language and Compiler for Tiled Neural Network Computations (http://www.eecs.harvard.edu/~htk/publication/2019-mapl-tillet-kung-cox.pdf). Please consider citing this work if you use Triton!'
findings.paper: Philippe Tillet, H. T. Kung, David Cox, "Triton: An Intermediate Language and Compiler for Tiled Neural Network Computations", MAPL 2019 (co-located with PLDI), pp. 10-19. DOI 10.1145/3315508.3329973
findings.verify_evidence: PLDI19/MAPL19 program page + conference-publishing.com ToC confirm title/authors/venue; DOI 10.1145/3315508.3329973.
findings.where_used: README.md:19 (cited in README, NOT in code/docs pages — foundational grounding for the entire book)
findings.grounding_rationale: The tile abstraction (statically-shaped multi-dim sub-arrays as the unit of program + IR) is the conceptual spine of the whole compiler. A short opening primer chapter on 'why tiles' anchors every later chapter.

findings.topic: Software pipeliner — modulo scheduling + prologue/epilogue expander
findings.mechanism_evidence: SoftwarePipeliner.cpp header: 'Software pipeliners are usually separated into two pieces, one that create a modulo schedule and an expander that rewrites the loop and emits a prologue and epilogue.' Schedule.cpp builds the stage/cluster schedule; PipelineExpander.cpp is a fork of the upstream MLIR loop pipeliner that peels prologue/epilogue. NO paper is cited anywhere in the Pipeliner/ directory.
findings.source_excerpt: lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/Pipeliner/SoftwarePipeliner.cpp:20-26 (modulo schedule + expander split); PipelineExpander.cpp:1-21 ('This file implements loop software pipelining' + 'Fork of upstream pipeliner')
findings.paper: B. Ramakrishna Rau, "Iterative Modulo Scheduling: An Algorithm for Software Pipelining Loops", MICRO-27, 1994, pp. 63-74. DOI 10.1145/192724.192731 (MICRO Test-of-Time 2016). Secondary lineage: Monica S. Lam, "Software Pipelining: An Effective Scheduling Technique for VLIW Machines", PLDI 1988, DOI 10.1145/53990.54022
findings.verify_evidence: ACM DL + HP Labs tech report HPL-94-115 confirm Rau MICRO-1994 title/pages; DOI 10.1145/192724.192731 resolves to the same. Lam PLDI'88 is the canonical companion.
findings.where_used: lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/Pipeliner/{SoftwarePipeliner.cpp,Schedule.cpp,PipelineExpander.cpp,MatmulLoopPipeline.cpp} — GAP: source uses 'modulo schedule' terminology but cites no reference
findings.grounding_rationale: The async/software-pipeline chapter (multi-stage prefetch of loads into shared memory overlapping the MMA) is unreadable without the modulo-scheduling model: initiation interval, stages, and prologue/epilogue peeling. This is exactly the classic pipelining theory applied to GPU loops.

findings.topic: LinearLayout: GF(2) linear maps as the universal layout algebra
findings.mechanism_evidence: include/triton/Tools/LinearLayout.h header derives the whole model: a layout L(t,w) is defined by its values on power-of-2 basis inputs and completed by the xor linearity rule L(t1⊕t2,w1⊕w2)=L(t1,w1)⊕L(t2,w2) — i.e. a linear map over GF(2). Composition/inversion/quotient are done by row-reduced echelon form over GF(2) (getMatrix + f2reduce). Header attributes the idea to Adam P. Goucher; there is NO academic paper.
findings.source_excerpt: include/triton/Tools/LinearLayout.h:18-20 '# High-level overview of linear layouts // The idea for linear layouts is due to Adam P. Goucher.' + :46 'L(t1 ⊕ t2, w1 ⊕ w2) = L(t1, w1) ⊕ L(t2, w2)  (linearity rule).'
findings.paper: No formal publication. Internal construction credited to Adam P. Goucher (Triton). Mathematical grounding = linear algebra over GF(2) (finite-field vector spaces); the RREF engine is the Four Russians method (see f2reduce entry).
findings.verify_evidence: Searched — no arXiv/DOI paper for 'Triton linear layout'. Source itself only credits an individual, not a publication. Recorded honestly rather than inventing a citation.
findings.grounding_rationale: LinearLayout unifies every register/thread/warp/shared layout in the compiler; it is a whole chapter. The primer must build GF(2)-linear-map intuition from the header's own worked example (the swizzle table) rather than cite a paper — pair it with the Four Russians box for the RREF machinery.

findings.topic: f2reduce: GF(2) Gaussian elimination (RREF) under LinearLayout
findings.mechanism_evidence: LinearLayout composition/pseudo-inverse call f2reduce::inplace_rref_strided on a bit-packed GF(2) matrix. third_party/f2reduce/README.md names the algorithm outright: 'Kronrod's algorithm (method of four Russians)'.
findings.source_excerpt: lib/Tools/LinearLayout.cpp:151,912,966 f2reduce::inplace_rref_strided(...); third_party/f2reduce/README.md 'It incorporates the following optimisations: - Kronrod\'s algorithm (\'method of four Russians\');'
findings.paper: V. L. Arlazarov, E. A. Dinic, M. A. Kronrod, I. A. Faradzhev, "On economical construction of the transitive closure of a directed graph", Soviet Mathematics Doklady 11 (1970), 1209-1210 (the 'Method of Four Russians')
findings.verify_evidence: Wikipedia/Grokipedia + Bard eprint 2006/251 confirm the four authors, 1970 Soviet Math Doklady origin, and the t×t block + lookup-table technique for GF(2) matrix ops.
findings.where_used: lib/Tools/LinearLayout.cpp (caller) — README names the algorithm (source-cited at the library level) but the LinearLayout caller gives no reference — GAP for the reader
findings.grounding_rationale: A 3-5 sentence box: 'layouts compose/invert by row-reducing a boolean matrix; f2reduce does GF(2) RREF fast via the Four Russians block-lookup trick.' Enough to demystify the f2reduce call without a full chapter.

findings.topic: AxisInfo: divisibility / contiguity / constancy dataflow analysis
findings.mechanism_evidence: lib/Analysis/AxisInfo.cpp defines a lattice over per-axis {divisibility (via extended-gcd), contiguity, constancy} and propagates it with mlir::DataFlowFramework (sparse forward monotone dataflow). Results drive vectorization / coalesced access. It is a textbook monotone dataflow analysis with a custom lattice — no citation in source.
findings.source_excerpt: lib/Analysis/AxisInfo.cpp:1 #include "mlir/Analysis/DataFlowFramework.h"; :17-40 extended-gcd; class AxisInfoVisitor + join/meet lattice ops over divisibility/contiguity
findings.paper: Gary A. Kildall, "A Unified Approach to Global Program Optimization", POPL 1973, pp. 194-206 (monotone-dataflow-lattice foundation). Companion formalization: J. B. Kam, J. D. Ullman, "Monotone Data Flow Analysis Frameworks", Acta Informatica 7 (1977), 305-317
findings.verify_evidence: Program-record + Semantic Scholar confirm Kildall POPL 1973 title/venue/pages 194-206; Kam-Ullman 1977 Acta Informatica is the standard monotone-framework reference.
findings.where_used: lib/Analysis/AxisInfo.cpp, include/triton/Analysis/AxisInfo.h — GAP: custom lattice, no reference
findings.grounding_rationale: A prereq box on 'monotone dataflow over a lattice, iterate to fixpoint' lets the reader see AxisInfo's divisibility/contiguity as one instance; the alignment reasoning itself is the interesting part and can be taught inline.

findings.topic: Shared-memory allocation: liveness + interference-graph coloring + offset bumping
findings.mechanism_evidence: lib/Analysis/Allocation.cpp computes shared-memory offsets by live-range analysis, builds an interference graph, colors it, then re-runs after 'bumping' offsets until a fixed point. The source cites the paper by title + DOI in a comment — a rare in-code citation.
findings.source_excerpt: lib/Analysis/Allocation.cpp:508-510 '/// Computes the shared memory offsets... /// Paper: Algorithms for Compile-Time Memory Optimization /// (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.5555/314500.315082)' + :552 'NOTE: The original paper doesn\'t consider interference between the bumped ranges...'
findings.paper: Jordan Gergov, "Algorithms for Compile-Time Memory Optimization", Proc. 10th Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) 1999, pp. 907-908. DOI 10.5555/314500.315082
findings.verify_evidence: Cited verbatim in Allocation.cpp; web-confirmed author (Jordan Gergov) + venue (SODA 1999) via ACM DL / Semantic Scholar for the 10.5555/314500.315082 record.
findings.where_used: lib/Analysis/Allocation.cpp (computeOffsets / interference graph) — cited in source
findings.grounding_rationale: Reader needs the intuition (memory buffers as intervals -> interference graph -> color/pack, then bump-and-recolor to a fixed point). The source even documents its deviation from the paper, which is a nice teaching hook. A box suffices; the code walk carries the rest.

findings.topic: FP8 element formats E4M3 / E5M2 (and FNUZ variants)
findings.mechanism_evidence: Type system + MMA legality reason over Float8E5M2 / Float8E4M3FN / Float8E4M3FNUZ / Float8E5M2FNUZ (MLIR builtin FP8 types). No spec/paper cited in source.
findings.paper: Paulius Micikevicius et al., "FP8 Formats for Deep Learning", 2022, arXiv:2209.05433 (defines E4M3 / E5M2). FNUZ ('finite, unsigned-zero') variants originate from Graphcore/AMD; documented in the OCP 8-bit FP work and LLVM APFloat.
findings.verify_evidence: arxiv.org/abs/2209.05433 -> title 'FP8 Formats for Deep Learning', Micikevicius et al., E4M3 (4-exp/3-mant) + E5M2 (5-exp/2-mant), E4M3 drops infinities/extends range. Matches the exact type set used in source.
findings.where_used: lib/Analysis/Utility.cpp, lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/{TypeConverter,ViewOpToLLVM}.cpp — GAP: uses named FP8 encodings without citing the format spec
findings.grounding_rationale: One box explaining sign/exp/mantissa bit budgets, why E4M3 for weights/acts vs E5M2 for grads, and the FN/FNUZ special-value differences; lets the reader follow the per-encoding MMA-legality and upcast tables.

findings.topic: Microscaling MXFP: block-scaled E2M1/E4M3/E5M2 with shared E8M0 scale (UpcastMXFPOp)
findings.mechanism_evidence: UpcastMXFPOp upcasts packed micro-scaled FP4/FP8 (F8F6F4Type::E2M1/E4M3/E5M2, E2M1 packs 2 elems/byte) using a per-block scale; AccelerateMatmul lowers scaled dot. This is the OCP MX block-float format. No spec cited in source.
findings.paper: OCP "Microscaling Formats (MX) Specification v1.0", Open Compute Project, 2023 (group size 32, shared E8M0 scale, MXFP8=E4M3/E5M2, MXFP6=E3M2/E2M3, MXFP4=E2M1). Academic companion: Bita Darvish Rouhani et al., "Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning", 2023, arXiv:2310.10537
findings.verify_evidence: opencompute.org OCP MX v1.0 spec page + arXiv:2310.10537 confirm the E2M1/E4M3/E5M2 element formats, group-of-32 + E8M0 shared scale — exactly the F8F6F4/UpcastMXFP shapes in source.
findings.where_used: lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/IR/Ops.cpp (UpcastMXFPOp), lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/AccelerateMatmul.cpp — GAP: implements MX upcast without citing the OCP spec
findings.grounding_rationale: Box: 'a block of 32 low-bit elements shares one E8M0 power-of-two scale; upcast = decode element * 2^scale.' Explains why UpcastMXFP takes a scale operand and why E2M1 packs two-per-byte.

findings.topic: MMA / TensorCore fragment layouts + shared-memory swizzle (Volta/Ampere/Hopper)
findings.mechanism_evidence: Dot lowering emits mma.sync / wgmma / ldmatrix and computes register-fragment layouts + shared-memory swizzles (32/64/128-byte) to avoid bank conflicts. Source references the NVIDIA PTX ISA docs by URL for the wgmma fragment layout; the swizzle geometry is vendor-defined, not academic.
findings.source_excerpt: lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/IR/Dialect.cpp:270-271 'Hopper MMA instructions force a warp order of [0, 1]. See docs: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html#matrix-fragments-for-wgmma-mma-async-m64nnk8'; LinearLayoutConversions.cpp:995-1053 swizzleByteSize 32/64/128
findings.paper: No academic paper — vendor specification: NVIDIA PTX ISA (mma.sync / wgmma.mma_async / ldmatrix; matrix-fragment layouts) and CUDA C++ Programming Guide (shared-memory bank-conflict / swizzle). Cited in source via docs.nvidia.com URL.
findings.verify_evidence: The docs.nvidia.com PTX-ISA URL is written verbatim in Dialect.cpp:271; these are vendor specs, so no arXiv/DOI applies (recorded honestly as spec, not a fabricated paper).
findings.where_used: lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/* (MMA lowering), lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/IR/{Dialect,LinearLayoutConversions}.cpp (fragment layouts + swizzle) — partly cited (PTX docs URL)
findings.grounding_rationale: Box on TensorCore MMA fragments (each thread holds a fixed slice of the tile) + why shared-memory is swizzled by XOR to spread accesses across 32 banks. Grounds the MMA-layout and swizzle chapters; the mechanism itself is engineering, not a paper.

findings.mechanism_evidence: python/triton/runtime/autotuner.py runs a plain benchmark-driven grid search over user-supplied Config list, with optional prune_configs_by hook. It implements no published autotuning algorithm — it is empirical best-of-N timing.
findings.source_excerpt: python/triton/runtime/autotuner.py: class Autotuner(..., configs, prune_configs_by, warmup, rep, ...) — brute-force do_bench over configs
findings.paper: None implemented (pure engineering). Broader autotuning lineage for optional context only: J. Ansel et al. 'OpenTuner' (PACT 2014); ATLAS (Whaley & Dongarra 1998). Source implements neither.
findings.verify_evidence: Read the source: it is a straightforward timed grid search, no algorithm from a paper. Listed for completeness; no citation asserted.
findings.grounding_rationale: Pure engineering (measure candidates, keep the fastest). No primer/paper needed; at most a one-line aside that Triton's autotuner is empirical, unlike learned/analytic autotuners.

primer_candidates: Triton tile abstraction (MAPL 2019) — foundational opening primer
Modulo scheduling (Rau MICRO'94) — required for the async/software-pipeline chapter
LinearLayout GF(2) algebra (no paper; internal) — its own chapter, paired with Four Russians box
prereq_box_candidates: Gergov SODA'99 memory allocation (Allocation.cpp, already source-cited)
OCP MX block-float (OCP MX v1.0 / arXiv:2310.10537)
NVIDIA PTX MMA fragments + swizzle (vendor spec)
summary_for_lead.gap_flags: Rau modulo scheduling, Kildall dataflow, FP8 formats, and OCP MX are used in source with NO citation — these are the true gap points a primer must cover. f2reduce/Four Russians is cited only in the third_party README, not at the LinearLayout call site.
